title: Rest from work
hookLine: your body has a right over you (Bukhari)
tomorrow: a gap in Amira's aid letter. if provision is written, why try?

lines: FAST EVERY DAY, PRAY ALL NIGHT.
cards: A note on the fridge: back Monday, doubles all week. Who tells a hard worker to stop? In one hadith, the Prophet ﷺ does, and the worker isn't slacking.
He's praying. A companion named 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr has taken on a heavy routine: fast every day, stand in prayer all night. Word reaches the Prophet, and he calls him in.
You'd expect praise. That's the odd part. He tells him to stop.

teach.h: FAST AND EAT, PRAY AND SLEEP.
teach.b: Here's what he says, in the report in Sahih al-Bukhari. Fast, and also eat. Stand in prayer, and also sleep.
Then the line this day is built on: your body has a right over you. Your eyes have a right over you.

teach.h: YOUR BODY HAS A RIGHT OVER YOU.
teach.b: Your wife has a right over you, and your guests have a right over you. That solves the puzzle. Rest isn't a break from doing right.
It's paying a debt. The body is owed something, the way a worker is owed a wage. Another report makes it sharper.
Salman visits his brother in faith, Abu al-Darda', and finds him fasting all day and praying all night.
Salman tells him: your Lord has a right on you, your self has a right on you, your family has a right on you, so give each its due. The Prophet hears it and says Salman spoke the truth.
The Qur'an builds rest into the shape of the day.
In Pickthall's words: "And have appointed your sleep for repose." Notice what got reined in here: extra worship.
So a double shift on a healing knee has a weak case. The tradition still prizes hard work; yesterday was all shovels. It just won't let the work eat the worker.
One for tonight: the man told to slow down was asking for more prayer, not less.

how: Muslims point to this hadith when work or extra worship starts to crowd out sleep, health and family: voluntary fasts and night prayers are kept in balance with the body's needs.

o: stopping to give the body the rest it is owed
the hours after work set aside for worship
a paid holiday that a boss gives to the staff

games.q: who said what about rest — tap the pairs.
p: fasted daily and prayed all night
have a right over you too

s: the Prophet praised the man who fasted every day and prayed all night
he told him to stop: fast and eat, pray and sleep.
the hadith says your body, your eyes, your wife and your guests each have a right over you
rest, sleep and the people around you are all owed something.
in Islam, rest is a reward you earn after enough work
the hadith calls it a right the body is owed, not a prize.

games.q: your friend has pulled two all-nighters for exams and plans a third. she says sleeping would be lazy. what does the hadith point to?
o: sleep tonight; her body has a right over her, and paying it isn't lazy.
push through; being worn out is a sign she's really trying.
a short nap, then keep going; any rest at all settles the debt.
games.why: the Prophet reined in a man doing extra worship: pray and sleep. if worship gets balanced with rest, an exam can be too.

practice: Let your body be the one that's owed. Unclench your jaw, drop your shoulders, and let your hands rest open on your legs. With each breath out, let one more muscle stop working, until the time is up.

wordCard.voice: Rest from work: giving the body the rest it's owed. In the hadith, the body has a right over you, like a wage.

orig.note: Arabic: a right, what is due. 'Your body has a haqq over you.'

carryVoice: Hold onto this: the body's right, owed like any wage, even on the busiest week. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1975 (also 5199, 6134: 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr told to fast and break the fast, pray and sleep; your body, your eyes, your wife and your guests have a right over you)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1968 (Salman and Abu al-Darda': give each its due; the Prophet: Salman spoke the truth)

sources.q: And have appointed your sleep for repose
